extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (especially philosophy of mathematics) seeking an overview of Wittgenstein's views
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedia entry summarizing Wittgenstein’s views on the nature, meaning, methods, and foundations of mathematics across his early, middle, and later periods, and presenting scholarly interpretation and critique. Useful for understanding his positions on formalism, finitism, decidability, set theory, and Gödel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractarian non-referential status of mathematical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Tractatus, mathematical propositions are not genuine (contingent) propositions; they are pseudo-propositions that are non-referential and purely syntactical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tautologies, contradictions and mathematical equations 'have no subject-matter', 'lack sense', and 'say nothing' about the world. Mathematical truth is not truth-by-correspondence but a feature of symbol manipulation within a calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as showing equivalence of meaning (method of substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs show that two expressions have the same meaning; correctness is manifest in the expressions themselves and proved by substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We 'prove' by seeing that two expressions are intersubstitutable; one can recognize the truth of logical and mathematical propositions by the symbol alone (e.g., substitution and symbol-manipulation suffice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidability of mathematical propositions by formal means
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical propositions are decidable by purely formal, syntactical means (calculations) rather than by appeal to external facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with contingent propositions whose truth depends on the world; mathematical 'truth-value' is a function of constituent symbols and the formal system they belong to.

rubrics_metrics.name: General-form theory (operations, propositions, numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical objects and propositions can be expressed by general forms (general form of an operation, of a proposition/truth-function, and of a natural number) modeled on formal variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein presents bracketed notations and variable-forms (e.g., [a,x,O⟙x], [ p,  , N()]) as the basis for generating series, truth-functions, and natural numbers by iteration/operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics as invention (formalism) — middle period core idea
rubrics_metrics.description: From c.1929 onward, Wittgenstein adopts a strong variant of formalism: 'we make mathematics' by inventing mathematical calculi with stipulated axioms, syntactical rules, and decision procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical truth and falsity are produced by algorithmic decision procedures within calculi; numbers and numerals are not proxies but are 'there' in the use (the numeral is the number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical meaning is intra-systemic (syntactical relations determine meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only meaning a mathematical proposition has is its intra-systemic meaning, wholly determined by syntactical relations to other propositions within the calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mathematics 'operates' with symbols rather than referring, to know what '2+2=4' means is to know how we work it out — the process of calculation is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-mathematical application not necessary for a mathematical calculus (middle Wittgenstein)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical calculi can be developed autonomously without needing extra-mathematical applications; application 'takes care of itself' where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittgenstein allows autonomous formal development of arithmetic while acknowledging that later he returns to the importance of extra-mathematical application to distinguish mere sign-games from genuine mathematical language-games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of infinite mathematical extensions (finitism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical extensions (symbols, finite sequences) are necessarily finite; an infinite mathematical extension (a completed infinite list) is a contradiction in terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mathematical infinite exists only as a recursive rule/intension ('and so on'), not as a completed extension. Talk of the 'whole infinite number series' as an extension is senseless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of unbounded quantification over infinite domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Because infinite mathematical extensions do not exist, one cannot meaningfully quantify over an infinite mathematical domain; expressions that do so are not genuine mathematical propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinite conjunctions or disjunctions (e.g., '(n) φ n' over all natural numbers) are not legitimate mathematical propositions; quantifiers over 'all numbers' lack bounded sense and thus are problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic decidability as constitutive of mathematical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: For Wittgenstein in the middle period, a mathematical proposition must either be proved/refuted within a calculus or be decidable by a known effective decision procedure; otherwise it is not a proposition of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He distinguishes proved, refuted, decidable (we know how), and non-propositions (no calculus applies). On his view, ordinary conjectures lacking known decision procedures (e.g., Goldbach) are senseless as mathematical propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-foundationalist account of real numbers: irrationals as rules (intensions), not extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational numbers are laws/rules (intensions) that 'yield extensions' rather than finite or completed infinite extensions; there is no set of all real numbers or continuum as a completed totality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because infinite sets are recursive rules and not extensions, the continuum and a completed set of real numbers do not exist as mathematical extensions on Wittgenstein's reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of different infinite cardinalities / critique of Cantor
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein rejects the standard interpretation of Cantor's diagonal argument as proving strictly greater infinite cardinalities, treating some set-theoretical moves as conceptual confusions arising from conflating intensions and extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mistake lies in treating laws (rules, inductions) and enumerations (lists, finite extensions) as the same kind of thing; 'infinite' is not a number-word in the same syntactic role as finite numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold classification of symbol-concatenations (proved/refuted/decidable/non-propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein distinguishes (1) proved propositions in a calculus, (2) refuted propositions, (3) propositions for which we have an applicable effective decision procedure, and (4) concatenations not part of any calculus (non-propositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is used to ground his position on decidability and to contrast his position with Brouwer's, especially concerning undecided propositions and the law of excluded middle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Excluded Middle is restricted / may not apply to expressions quantifying over infinite domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein holds that expressions quantifying over infinite domains may invalidate the ordinary application of the Law of Excluded Middle, rendering such expressions senseless rather than genuine mathematical propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because undecidable 'propositions' without known decision procedures lack sense, the classical law (p ∨ ¬p) doesn't automatically apply to them; this is central to his finitistic constructivism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later Wittgenstein: mathematics as human invention and anti-Platonism
rubrics_metrics.description: In his later work Wittgenstein emphasizes mathematics as a human invention and offers an anti-Platonic account: numbers and mathematical practices are grounded in human forms of life and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He develops the 'natural history of numbers' and stresses that Platonism is vacuous if detached from human practices; this reframes the question of mathematical objectivity and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later Wittgenstein: extra-mathematical application as necessary for mathematical meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: In later writings Wittgenstein treats extra-mathematical application (use outside pure sign-games) as a necessary condition for mathematical meaningfulness, distinguishing mere sign-games from genuine language-games of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications and uses outside the calculus help determine whether a formal scheme counts as mathematics; this is a development from his earlier allowance of autonomous calculi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later critique of set theory: intensions vs extensions and the fictitious symbolism of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein criticizes set-theoretical practices that treat laws and enumerations alike, denouncing certain set-theoretical symbolism as fictitious and conceptually misleading (e.g., issues of non-denumerability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns against reifying syntactic devices into metaphysical entities and stresses careful attention to grammar and the different roles of rules vs lists in mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of Gödel — questioning the significance of undecidable propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein offers a critical and controversial take on Gödel's incompleteness results: he challenges the standard import of 'undecidable' sentences, denying that undecidable formulae are necessarily mathematical propositions of existing calculi without decision procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry summarizes debates and interpretations of Wittgenstein's remarks on Gödel; Wittgenstein denies 'unknown truths' in mathematics and regards claims about undecidable propositions as indicative of misapplied grammar or of working outside a calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical operations and iteration generate number series (successive applications ≡ 'and so on')
rubrics_metrics.description: Wittgenstein models natural numbers and certain mathematical constructions as successive applications of general forms/operations; the infinite is captured by the potential to iterate, not by completed infinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general form [0, ξ, ξ+1] and related operational schemas show how numbers are generated by repetition of an operation; the infinite is an 'infinite possibility' rather than a completed collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical propositions are used instrumentally in inferences between contingent propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when conceived as formal, mathematical propositions are often employed to mediate inferences from non-mathematical (contingent) propositions to other contingent propositions; this instrumental role distinguishes mere sign-games from applied mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Tractatus Wittgenstein notes we use mathematics in inferences between factual claims; later he refines when such usage renders a formalism genuinely mathematical (requires application and grammar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful attention to grammatical/category mistakes in mathematical language
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring Wittgensteinian criterion is that philosophical errors about mathematics often stem from grammatical-category confusions (e.g., treating 'infinite' as a number-word, conflating rules and lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of Wittgenstein's critique of set theory, infinite cardinals, and certain interpretations of quantification is diagnostic: identify the grammatical misuses that generate pseudo-problems.
